metadata.title: Solve-Verify Asymmetry — AI Thinks Fast, Verification Thinks Harder
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: an AI can produce an answer fast, but for hard problems confirming that answer is correct costs far more — checking is the harder half of the job, and a faster model does not shrink that gap. Lands the carry-out that speed at solving does not buy speed at checking.
metadata.anchor_pair: B01 -> B06 (the ratio ladder: arithmetic/algebra/quadratic/combinatorics, planted with raw ratios, returns corrected after the measurement-artifact fix, plus a proof-sketch rung that overflows the chart)

beats.narration_text: Someone assumes that if Claude solves a problem in seconds, checking the answer must be just as fast. It isn't — for hard problems, checking can take far longer. So: is checking fast, or harder?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Claude solved it. In two seconds. So checking is fast, right?', hesitates on 'fast', corrects to 'harder'

props.text:
Claude solved it
in two seconds.
So checking is fast,
right?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. Single-word trigger ('fast') swapped for a single-word replacement ('harder') so buildActs()'s whitespace-token match fires. TIMING LAW: 34-word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('fast' -> 'harder') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Try it yourself: ten problems of rising difficulty, timed two ways — how fast the AI answers, and how long a strict, deterministic check takes to confirm it. Divide the two. Simple arithmetic: the check ran about three times as long as the answer. Hard combinatorics: about a hundred times.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR - a ratio ladder, four rungs, raw measured ratios

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR - the ratio ladder
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. Four stacked rungs labeled ARITHMETIC, ALGEBRA, QUADRATIC, COMBINATORICS, each a growing bar with its ratio value (3x, 20x, 40x, 100x) filled in one at a time. THIS EXACT LADDER COMPOSITION RETURNS AT B06.

beats.narration_text: The natural guess: since the AI already produced the answer, confirming it should be just as fast — glance at the same work, done.

shot.new_visual_element: Fast in, fast out - mirrored arrows around one answer box

production_viz.label: The natural guess - fast in, fast out
production_viz.mechanic: An ANSWER card in the center. An arrow labeled 'SOLVE — fast' points into it from the left. A mirrored arrow labeled 'CONFIRM — fast?' points away from it to the right, drawn the same length and speed as the first, suggesting parity.

beats.narration_text: But the measured ratios break that guess — checking took three to a hundred times longer, not the same. For many hard problems, producing one plausible answer is comparatively cheap; actually confirming it's correct means doing the real computation over — and that's the expensive part.

shot.new_visual_element: The mirrored arrows struck through; two paths at different costs, GUESS vs CONFIRM

production_viz.label: The break - confirm is not a mirror of solve
production_viz.mechanic: The B02 mirrored-arrow pair reappears, struck through in terracotta. Beneath it, two separate paths: a short cheap arrow labeled 'GUESS a candidate' and a long, thick arrow labeled 'CONFIRM it — redo the computation', visibly unequal in length.

beats.narration_text: One number looked wrong: three times seemed too low for arithmetic — checking should barely cost anything there. The culprit was a hidden startup cost in the checker itself. Strip that out, and arithmetic ties out close to one-to-one. Algebra, quadratic, and combinatorics don't move at all — the gap there was never a measurement artifact.

shot.new_visual_element: A checker box with a hidden startup-cost weight removed; arithmetic bar shrinking to parity, other bars unmoved

production_viz.label: The rigor check - is the gap real, or the stopwatch?
production_viz.mechanic: A CHECKER box with a small labeled weight, 'hidden startup cost', attached to it. The weight is struck and removed. Beside it, a small arithmetic bar shrinks from 3x down to touch a 1x marker line, while three other small bars (algebra/quadratic/combinatorics) stay exactly where they were.

beats.narration_text: One direction: a big ratio on a hard problem doesn't mean the AI's answer was wrong — it only means confirming correctness costs more, whether the answer is right or not.

shot.new_visual_element: A ratio number boxed as cost-to-confirm; a separate faded card 'right or wrong?' outside the box

production_viz.label: A ratio only measures the cost to confirm
production_viz.mechanic: A bounded box labeled 'COST TO CONFIRM' containing a large ratio number. Outside the box's dashed boundary, a separate faded card reads 'right or wrong?' with a question mark — visibly untouched by the box.

beats.narration_text: The other direction: a faster AI model doesn't close this gap — it can widen it, since more candidate answers arrive per second, and each one still needs the same expensive check. Redo the ladder after the fix: arithmetic near one-to-one, algebra and combinatorics unchanged, and a full proof sketch runs about three hundred times longer to check than to produce — off the chart.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS - same ladder, corrected arithmetic rung, a fifth proof rung overflowing the chart

production_viz.label: The anchor returns - corrected ladder, plus proof
production_viz.mechanic: THE B01 LADDER COMPOSITION RETURNS, identical layout. The arithmetic rung's bar shrinks to near-parity (ghost of the old 3x bar fades beneath it); algebra/quadratic/combinatorics bars are unchanged. A fifth rung, PROOF SKETCH, is added: its bar runs past the right edge of the chart with an overflow arrow and the label '~300x'.

beats.narration_text: For hard problems, checking an answer costs far more than producing one — and a faster model doesn't close that gap, it just produces more answers that still need checking.

props.quote: For hard problems, checking an answer costs far more than producing one — and a faster model doesn't close that gap, it just produces more answers that still need checking.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. I want to measure the solve-verify gap in my own work. Walk me through picking three tasks I do with AI — one trivial, one medium, one hard — and timing a deterministic check against how long the AI took to answer. What should I do differently if that ratio turns out to be large? Liam, in for Bear.
